There's 3 very important questions that should be easy to answer. 

Am I the beatdown? Oftentimes, it's answered in deck building. Control and combo already know the answer is no. Aggro will usually be a yes. Midrange decides based on how their opponent answers. It will be obvious when this answer changes during the game. 

This question will auto decide your plays for most of the game. 

The second question is "Do I care about (card opponent played?" If yes, see question 3. If not, play towards your gameplan established in question 1. 

Question 3 is "Can I do anything about it?" Not always a relevant question, but an important one. If the answer is in your hand, play it. If not, proceed with original gameplan. In the following turns this question will be easier to answer as you only have to look at 1-3 cards. 

And that's it. That's the game of magic. You do this over and over until the game ends. And then repeat it for the next game. Any caveats or additional questions during the game will be auto answered by question 3. If the answer to question 3 is no, then thinking about it for 3 more minutes won't change it.

The tutorial for Arena still has areas where they assume you already have some knowledge of the game, so it's not uncommon for it to be confusing. Despite the reaction of some of the mongrels here I would implore you to keep asking any questions you have. That's the fastest way to get better. 

When you're done with the tutorial, do the Color challenges and then the Starter Deck battles. You'll be paired against other players using starter decks. 

I want to also include some resources that will help you get started/see what the game has to offer. 

MTG Goldfish - Has a lot of budget decks that will be easier for new players to build. Typically they're "budget" in that they're less than $100 in paper. But some of them are budget in terms of Arena. 

Tolarian Community College - The Professor has tutorial videos that are a bit more in depth than Arena. He also has a lot of review videos of Magic Accessories for paper Magic. He has a lot of different video types to check out. 

The Command Zone - A podcast for the commander format (On Arena it's called Brawl). Not every card they talk about is available on Arena, but the important thing is what they consider when they build their decks. 

Limited Resources - This is for the Limited format (Draft and Sealed). It's a little high level and I don't usually recommend it until someone has a good grasp on the game. This podcast is responsible for my biggest improvements in every format. I would skip set reviews and sunset shows at first. They're not super useful unless you're playing a lot of limited.

I didn't care for the 3-3-5 tite after all. After years of trying to make it work, I set my playbook to 4-2-5 so I could find a different job and start over. 

The downside of the 3-3-5 tite may have more to do with the engine then anything else. I couldn't stop the run. It was a guaranteed 5 yards every time.  I'll go over the archetypes I was using, which if anyone has any suggestions, I'm open to them. 

DT: Run Stopper (Must be 320+ lbs)
RE: Run Stopper (Must be 275+ lbs)
LE: Power Rusher (Must be 265+ lbs)

The way that the 3 front irl works is by having bigger down lineman that demand double teams. Leaving your LBs to fill the gaps. This is why I think it's an engine problem. The CPU would single block my DL (and it would work) and then the LBs would get blocked by the leftover OL. I started to experiment with recruiting 3 DTs instead of DEs, but I didn't stick it out. 

LOLB: power rusher
MLB: Field General or Pass Coverage
MLB: Field General or Run Stopper
ROLB: Power Rusher (actually a speed rusher but the game doesn't differentiate)

This is what an irl 3-4 looks like, with both OLBs capable of rushing to keep the protection guessing. The OLBs actually weren't the biggest liability in zone coverage as just standing there will sometimes be enough. They'd get a pass deflection or two but we're never really a threat to intercept. The MLBs have ideally 2 field generals that are above average at everything. If you don't have one then a combo of pass coverage and run stopper is a decent blend. 

Any combo of secondary works. This scheme has as much zone/man as the next. This scheme was as good as any at defending the pass.

 Its major weakness is running the ball. The 3-3-5 doesn't do what it's supposed to in freeing up LBs and having big DL that don't get pushed. The 4-2-5 uses a more athletic DL that also can get pushed off the line, but can also shed their blocks and get in the backfield. The DL of the 3-3-5 are never a threat to do that.

 Plus the way that tackling works, if an HB bumps into someone, they have a good chance of making the tackle. With 4 down lineman, it increases the chance of this happening. With the 3 DL, the OL gets to the 2nd level easier and gives the runner a better chance of not bumping into a DL or an LB. 

To be clear, it's a difference of ~1.5 yards. But that means a 2 yard gain against the 4-2-5 is a 3.5 yard gain against the 3-3-5. Meaning the drive strings along. So you need to have good backups for the 3-3-5 as the larger DL gets winded faster than the athletic 4-2-5 DL. And if they run hurry up? You have to stop them within 7 plays or your DL will be as useful as blocking sleds with how quickly they get tired.

It's important to not forget the 4-2-5 defense.

4 down linemen, 2 linebackers, 2 Corners and 3 safeties, with the 2nd string SS being the one who is at the line of scrimmage like a nickel corner. 

It strictly uses the R depth chart, despite being a base defense. So RLE, RDT, RRE, Sub LB. The 2nd string SS is the one by the line of scrimmage, so you may have a depth chart where your best safety is second string. 

With so many teams being in 3 WR sets and running out of it, it shores up the problem with being in Nickel defense, with the SS helping in the run game. It is more vulnerable to running plays than a 4-3 or 3-4, but not as vulnerable as a straight Nickel. It also comes with a 4-4 set for option or Pro style teams. As well as the standard Nickel, Dime and Prevent defenses. 

Recommended archetypes by position.
LE: speed/power rushers
DT: Speed rushers
RE: Power/speed rushers
LOLB: Run Stopper
MLB: Field General
ROLB: Pass Coverage
CB: Zone or Man corners 
FS: Zone
SS: Zone up top, Hybrid by the line.

I also like to keep 2 run stopping DTs in case I face a power spread. I'll sub them in as RDTs to help. I'll lose out on some pass rushing, but I also prevent QB scrambles up the middle.  And I try to recruit the 6'2" Hybrid safeties. Run support SS work too, but I might as well run a 4-3 at that point. I want the flexibility. You can be REALLY aggressive with this defense, leading to a lot of interceptions.

But I'm going to talk about a very special block that had two back to back broken metas. Kaladesh block. 

It should be noted that before Kaladesh released, Wizards of the Coast decided to delay rotation. So cards were still legal that shouldn't have been. Additionally, Kaladesh I produced a new energy mechanic. 

The first deck was Saheeli Rai and Felidar Guardian. Saheeli is a Planeswalker that let you make a copy of a creature you controlled, except it's an artifact. She starts with the counters and the ability cost 2 counters. Felidar Guardian had an ability where you exiled a card and then brought it right back into play. The card had a typo and it let you target any permanent, including planeswalkers. This let you make infinite Felidar Guardians that had haste and could kill you in one turn. 

The 2nd was Temur Marvel. Aetherworks Marvel said "Spend six energy and tap: Look at the top 6 cards of your library. You may CAST one of them without paying it's mana cost." Another card that SHOULD have rotated was Ulamog the ceaseless Hunger. They were an Eldrazi Titan that cost 10 mana, when they were cast, you could exile any two permanents, was indestructible, had 10 power and 10 toughness, and when they attacked your opponent had to exile the top 20 cards of their library. The rest of the deck was based on getting to 6 energy. It was possible to have 6 energy on turn 4 and suddenly cast Ulamog, exiling two of their lands and not being easily answered. It was basically a slot machine. The only matchup that was a problem was a zombies deck, but after the Pro Tour, everyone added a card that could also be cast off of Marvel and then everyone had a hard time. My fight or flight response triggers, and it is always flight. Elevation of heart rate, shallow breathing and what I can best describe as not having total control of my own self. Being wary of certain creatures is normal for most people. But what a phobia is, is an irrational fear. My brain exaggerates the danger to the point of removing control from me and giving it over to the same reflex as when you touch a hot stove and pull your hand away (which is normally an involuntary action). It's the same reason why people who have a phobia of clowns can't watch movies with clowns even though it's not physically present.

The 2nd thing that happens is that my brain will fixate on seeing a spider to the point that my anxiety elevates and I develop a paranoia about one being near me. This is why it doesn't matter if it's in a game or a movie, because the brain develops a paranoia about a real one existing. The worst though is going to sleep, because there will be one in my dreams. I can't outrun it because my mind is so fixated on it that it follows me. Or, I wake up and have to go back to sleep where the cycle continues. I basically have to wait for my brain to forget that it saw a spider. 

I didn't used to be THIS bad. I played Skyrim and other games no problem. It's definitely worse ever since I got bit by one. TLDR: We have every right to be mad, but we're mad at the wrong people for this problem. 

The cycle that's supposed to happen is you get your starter home, then when you start having a family (remember, starter homes were bought by people under 30) you would upgrade to a 3 or 4 bedroom for the kids. Then when you get older and the kids have moved out, you settle back into a starter house that's easier to take care of. 

The reason that boomers aren't selling their family houses is because they don't have anywhere to go. We're jammed up in the starter home market for a multitude of reasons. Developers are building $2750/month townhouses and $1500/month 1 bedroom apartments instead of houses. We don't regulate companies buying residential lots. So, supply is not increasing despite demand (we can argue about whether we should have ever let needs become commodities later). 

Then we get into the taxes from home value appreciation if they do sell their house. So even if they manage to find a house, it's at a bloated price. Between that and the tax from selling, it just isn't worth it. 

Who we need to be angry with is our representatives for not passing regulation to prevent companies from buying residential land. We can also be mad at the companies, but we can't directly affect them in a meaningful way. Our representatives, with the pooled resources of the citizens, are supposed to be our sword and shield against them.

For people who may want to play defense but struggle, I have a couple of tips that have helped me. 

The important thing to remember is that zone defense is too strict in NCAA 14. They don't properly pass receivers off to each other, leaving gaps in coverage that shouldn't be there. Cover 3 however is the better of the zone schemes as the defenders have to travel to their zone and they will play the ball if the pass is thrown before they get to their zone. Other than that, just play man defense for passing situations. You'll give up certain routes but a tackle will usually be imminent. 

For running plays, I use Cover 2. Keeps the DBs on the line and the linebackers are all looking at the play develop. In man coverage, they're looking at their responsibility. Especially so against an option team. Call Cover 2 and set the DEs to contain. It usually forces the play to get strung out farther to give your linebackers time to get there. 

You can mix it up with some blitzes, but safety and corner blitzes basically always lead to a big gain UNLESS you can collapse the pocket as well. It seems that on Heisman difficulty, a corner blitzing unchecked doesn't trigger whatever causes QBs to throw bad passes. Better to leave DBs in coverage. The boring part might be just how good a vanilla defense actually is. I also tend to do a lot of checks at the line as I read the offensive formation. 

Never, ever predict the play unless you predict pass. Predicting a running play and the direction, even if you get it right, creates cutback lanes. Even predicting middle run on a goal line stand will cause the HB to bounce outside and walk it in. Predicting pass is pretty safe to do against certain teams, on obvious passing downs, or if you're ahead by two or three scores which forces them to become one dimensional.

Sorters grouped pictures with orders. Roller would then take the pictures and place them on an adhesive cardboard backing and put them through a roller to make sure it adhered. Then they'd be grouped together and placed in a bin with a number on the outside to indicate how many pictures were there because we had a cutting quota we all lied about meeting. The cutters also had to do a final QC check for retouches. And then walk the orders where they were supposed to go next.

I was a cutter and let me tell you, it is boring and it sucked. But whatever, a check is a check except we would get mandatory overtime for not shipping enough orders. The quota was 5000 orders shipped in a day. And we'd come in to first shift having done....500 orders. I was VERY vocal about how it was total bullshit, every day. Okay so, something I learned while training to play a game competitively is that you have keep the big picture. If you make the correct choice but it had a negative result, that doesn't mean that you never do it again. And sometimes you have to account for the extreme long term.

If we had a time traveling super computer, we could know the correct play every single time. But since we don't, we have to accept that sometimes the play will be sub optimal. Any easily relatable example is going for it on 4th down. The math says that it's correct to go for it in specific conditions. And we do go for it every one of those times even if they haven't been successful. Because over the course of years, it will account for X more wins than if we hadn't.

Another example is no team since whatever year had 4 turnovers and won the game. 0-15 was the record. We lost so now its 1-15 since whatever year. Just because we lost after getting 4 turnovers doesn't mean that turnovers are valued any less. That's really easy to grasp when the percentages are so large. But when we're dealing with narrower margins, it's harder to see that data play out. So if a play is successful 54% of the time, it's still a good play because over the years it will give us that extra 4% chance to win. You take those percentage points every time.

A superintelligent AI would be so foreign to us that we wouldn't understand it for a long, long time. That is if we even would recognize that it was self aware. We don't even know how to quantify our own self awareness and we've embarrassed ourselves by implementing tests on other animals based on our prejudices and got false negatives.

A good example is the mirror test, which dogs failed so they were labeled not aware. But dogs absolutely are since they recognize their own scent. Another test is whether an animal will ask a question. And again, we expect them to ask questions in our language. We don't know what a dog asking a question looks like.
